newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian OLOs shift to range-bound mode.
newsitem.headline: Belgian OLOs shift to range-bound mode.

text.p: Belgian government bonds (OLOs) went into range-bound mode on Friday after a set of mixed data on the U.S. labour market in March, which was initially shrugged off and then on a re-assessment triggered some light selling.

Payrolls numbers came out slightly lower than forecast, but the jobless rate fell to a cyclical low and average hourly earnings grew relatively strongly, pointing to a tight market and possible future inflationary pressures, dealers said.
The sell-off was mild, however, and in thin volume, leading dealers to the conclusion that the bond market would stabilise at around current levels.

"It is stabilisation from here on...there will not be any major moves until the Fed (Federal Open Market Committee, which sets interest rate policy) meeting in May...until then the 10-year benchmark (yield) will move between 6.10 and 6.35 percent," a trader said.
The benchmark yielded 6.18 percent at 1440 GMT, unchanged from Thursday's late level, but up from 6.16 earlier on Friday.

Dealers said that while the U.S. jobs data had not removed any concerns about another U.S. rate rise, the economic cycles in Europe and the U.S. were such that there was no immediate need for European central banks to follow suit.
"The prospects here are different from the U.S. Economies are recovering slowly, but there will not be a need for higher rates here until the end of this year or early next year," he said.

In Europe "the rate cycle has not yet turned here," one trader said. "I can't see market rates rising much further here, it's improbable, with the German benchmark yield at 6.05 percent and inflation at 2.5 percent we have reached the ceiling."
The Bundesbank, and in its wake the Belgian central bank, would not raise short-term interest rates any time soon. "There is no reason to," he said.

Some analysts have forecast the yield on the 10-year benchmark would edge down to 6.00 percent or 5.90 by the end of the second quarter to reflect sluggish economic growth and a lack of major inflationary pressures.
